> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

derivations.claim: For each integer $m\ge1$, tightness and [A1] give a compact set $K_m\subset B$ with $\mu(K_m)>1-2^{-m}$. Each compact metric space $K_m$ has a countable dense subset: for each integer $r\ge1$, compactness gives a finite $1/r$-net, and the union of these finite nets is countable and dense. The union over $m$ of these dense subsets is countable; let $S$ be its closure. Then $S$ is separable, contains every $K_m$, and $\mu(S)\ge\mu(K_m)>1-2^{-m}$ for every $m$, hence $\mu(S)=1$.

Let $E$ be the closed real linear span of $S$. Rational linear combinations of a countable dense subset of $S$ form a countable dense subset of its real linear span, so $E$ is separable; it is closed by construction and therefore Banach, and $\mu(E)=1$. Define $W_E=W$ on the measurable event $\{W\in E\}$ and $W_E=0$ on its null complement. Then $W_E$ is $E$-valued and Borel measurable: each Borel set of $E$ is $E\cap A$ for some ambient Borel $A$, and its preimage is $\{W\in E\}\cap W^{-1}(A)$ together with the null complement if the set contains zero. Its law is the restriction of $\mu$ to $E$. For any $\ell\in E^*$, let $p(x)=\|\ell\|_{E^*}\|x\|_B$ on $B$; $\ell$ is dominated by $p$ on $E$. By [A2] it extends to a linear $\widetilde\ell$ on $B$ dominated by $p$, and applying domination to $x$ and $-x$ gives $|\widetilde\ell(x)|\le\|\ell\|_{E^*}\|x\|_B$. Since $W_E=W$ almost surely, $\ell(W_E)=\widetilde\ell(W)$ almost surely, so $\ell(W_E)$ is centered normal. Thus the restricted law is Gaussian.

For tightness in $E$, replace each compact $K_m$ by $K_m\cap E$, which is compact and has the same $\mu$-mass because $\mu(E)=1$. If $x\notin E$, closedness gives a $B$-open neighborhood disjoint from $E$, of $\mu$-mass zero, so $x$ is outside the ambient support. If $x\in E$, every ambient open ball about $x$ intersects $E$ in an $E$-open neighborhood and has the same measure as that intersection; hence all such neighborhoods have positive measure exactly when all relative neighborhoods do. The two supports therefore agree.

> ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $p,q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable densities with $\int p\,d\mu=\int q\,d\mu=1$. They define probability laws $P(B)=\int_Bp\,d\mu$ and $Q(B)=\int_Bq\,d\mu$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **root-L2 Hellinger distance**, with the root-L2 normalization, is
$$h(P,Q):=\left(\int_{\mathsf X}(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\,d\mu\right)^{1/2}.$$

The dominating measure $\mu$ is fixed throughout a use of this definition. Changing either density on a $\mu$-null set does not change the value, since the integrand changes only on a null set. This definition does not assert that separate choices of density versions are jointly measurable in an additional parameter.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, and suppose $f$ has derivatives through order $n+1$ on the closed interval between $a$ and $x$, with the usual endpoint continuity. If $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ throughout that interval, then
$$|R_{n,a}f(x)|\le \frac{M}{\iota((n+1)!)}|x-a|^{n+1}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which

every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

measurable for each $i<n$.

   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$

   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same

Exponential Markov [F3] with $\lambda=n^2t/(\sigma^2\sum_i c_i^2)$ bounds each one-sided tail by $\exp(-nt^2/(2\sigma^2\|c\|_n^2))$; if all $c_i=0$, the statistic is identically zero.

By [F4], for $|x|\le1/2$, $-x-\log(1-x)\le x^2$: for $x\ge0$ integrate $u/(1-u)\le2u$ on $[0,x]$, and for $x<0$ integrate $u/(1+u)\le u$ on $[0,|x|]$. Exponential Markov [F3] and step 1.2 give the upper tail $\exp(-nt^2/(4V_b))$; applying the same argument to the negative centered sum gives the lower tail. Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$
be real-valued, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval containing $f(x)$ for
almost every $x$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$ be convex with
$\varphi\circ f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$. Then
$$\varphi\!\left(\int f\,d\mathbb P\right)\le\int\varphi(f)\,d\mathbb P.$$

For a finite family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ of square-integrable real random variables on one common probability space,
$$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}X_i\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{Var}(X_i)+2\sum_{\{i,j\}\subseteq I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j).$$
Equivalently, it is $\sum_{i,j\in I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$. The empty sum has variance zero, and the singleton formula is the identity.
The original finite-probability-space case is included, since every real random variable there is square-integrable and the covariance/variance definitions agree with the finite centered-product/square formulas.
In the first display, the second sum is over two-element subsets of $I$.

and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: On the $P_0^{(n)}$-full set where every $p_{i0}(Y_i)$ is positive and finite, put $R_n(\theta)=\prod_i p_{i\theta}(Y_i)/p_{i0}(Y_i)$. For fixed $\theta$, independence [F1]–[F2] gives $E_0R_n(\theta)=\prod_i\int_{\{p_{i0}>0\}}p_{i\theta}\,d\mu_i\le1.$ Tonelli [F6] then gives $E_0D_n\le1$, so $D_n<\infty$ almost surely.

Let $\Pi_{K_n}$ be $\Pi$ conditioned on $K_n$ and set $Z_n=\int_{K_n}\sum_i\log\frac{p_{i\theta}(Y_i)}{p_{i0}(Y_i)}\,\Pi_{K_n}(d\theta).$ Tonelli [F6] applied to the log-ratio squares gives integrability over the conditional prior and sample space; the inequality $|u|\le1+u^2$ also makes the log ratios jointly integrable. Thus their conditional-prior integrals have measurable finite versions almost surely, and Jensen [F3] makes them square-integrable. Directional KL gives $E_0Z_n\ge-n\epsilon_n^2$. Writing $Z_n=\sum_iV_i(Y_i)$, independence [F1] and [F4] give $\operatorname{Var}_0 Z_n\le\sum_iE_0V_i(Y_i)^2$. Jensen [F3] applied to the conditional prior integral yields $E_0V_i(Y_i)^2\le\int_{K_n}E_{i0}\!\left[\left(\log\frac{p_{i\theta}(Y_i)}{p_{i0}(Y_i)}\right)^2\right]\Pi_{K_n}(d\theta),$ so $\operatorname{Var}_0 Z_n\le n\epsilon_n^2$.

Chebyshev [F5] implies $P_0^{(n)}\{Z_n<-2n\epsilon_n^2\}\le1/(n\epsilon_n^2)$, since $E_0Z_n\ge-n\epsilon_n^2$ and $\operatorname{Var}_0Z_n\le n\epsilon_n^2$. Jensen for $\log$ gives $D_n\ge\int_{K_n}R_n(\theta)\Pi(d\theta)\ge\Pi(K_n)\exp(Z_n).$ On the complementary event, this is at least $e^{-(C+2)n\epsilon_n^2}$. Together with step 1.1 this proves the claim.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be independent $N(0,1)$ variables, let $c_1,\ldots,c_n,\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_n\in\mathbb R$, and let $0<\sigma\le b$. Put $\|c\|_n^2=n^{-1}\sum_i c_i^2$ and $\|\delta\|_n^2=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_i^2$. For $t>0$,
$$\Pr\!\left(\left|n^{-1}\sum_i c_i\sigma Z_i\right|\ge t\right)\le2\exp\!\left(-\frac{nt^2}{2\sigma^2\|c\|_n^2}\right),$$
with zero probability when $\|c\|_n=0$. If $\|\delta\|_n\le1$ and $0<t\le b^2+2$, then
$$\Pr\!\left(\left|n^{-1}\sum_i(\delta_i+\sigma Z_i)^2-(\sigma^2+\|\delta\|_n^2)\right|\ge t\right)\le2\exp\!\left(-\frac{nt^2}{4V_b}\right),\qquad V_b=2b^4+4b^2.$$

law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, and let $H\subseteq B$ be its covariance RKHS. Define
$\operatorname{supp}\mu$ to be the set of $x\in B$ for which every open
neighborhood has positive $\mu$-measure. Then
$$\operatorname{supp}\mu=\overline H^{\,B}.$$

Assume AC and countable choice. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, with covariance RKHS $H$, and let $w_0\in\overline H^{\,B}$. For
$\varepsilon>0$, write
$\varepsilon B^\circ=\{x\in B:\|x\|_B<\varepsilon\}$ and define the
**concentration function**
$$\phi_{w_0}(\varepsilon) =\inf_{\substack{h\in H\\\|h-w_0\|_B<\varepsilon}} \left\{\|h\|_H^2-\log\mu(\varepsilon B^\circ)\right\}.$$
The feasible set is nonempty because $w_0$ lies in the Banach-norm closure of
$H$. Also $\mu(\varepsilon B^\circ)>0$ because $0\in\operatorname{supp}\mu$;
thus the logarithm is finite. The value is finite and nonnegative. The support assertion used here is
[[thm-support-of-banach-gaussian-is-closure-of-rkhs]].

Assume AC and countable choice. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian
law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, with covariance RKHS $H$, and let $w_0\in\overline H^{\,B}$.
Suppose $n\ge1$, $\varepsilon>0$, $C>1$,
$e^{-Cn\varepsilon^2}<1/2$, and
$\phi_{w_0}(\varepsilon)\le n\varepsilon^2$, where $\phi_{w_0}$ is the
concentration function. Then there is a measurable set $B_n\subseteq B$
such that
$$\log N(3\varepsilon,B_n,\|\cdot\|_B)\le6Cn\varepsilon^2,\qquad \mu(B\setminus B_n)\le e^{-Cn\varepsilon^2},$$
and
$$\mu\{\|W-w_0\|_B<2\varepsilon\}\ge e^{-n\varepsilon^2}.$$
These are prior-mass and sieve bounds only; they assert no posterior
contraction without separate statistical-distance and Kullback–Leibler
comparisons.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let $B$ be a real
separable Banach space with its norm Borel sigma-algebra. A map
$W:\Omega\to B$ is a **centered Borel Gaussian random element** if it is
Borel-measurable and, for every $\ell\in B^*$, the real random variable
$\ell(W)$ has a centered (possibly zero-variance) normal law. Its law is the
Borel probability $\mu=P\circ W^{-1}$. When the word *tight* is used, it means
that for every $\delta>0$ there is a norm-compact $K\subseteq B$ with
$\mu(K)>1-\delta$.

This definition concerns a random element in $B$. A Gaussian process on an
arbitrary index set with only a cylinder-space law does not satisfy it unless
a Borel $B$-valued realization is separately constructed.

Assume AC. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random element in a real separable
Banach space $B$, with law $\mu$. For $\ell\in B^*$ define
$$C\ell=E[\ell(W)W]\in B,\qquad Q(\ell,m)=E[\ell(W)m(W)]\quad(\ell,m\in B^*).$$
The **Cameron–Martin reproducing-kernel Hilbert space** $H$ is the completion
of $B^*/N$ in the inner product induced by $Q$, where
$N=\{\ell\in B^*:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$. The canonical map sends the class of
$\ell$ to $C\ell$ and extends continuously to an injective map $i:H\to B$;
we identify $H$ with its image in $B$ and use the completed Hilbert norm
$\|\cdot\|_H$. The preceding construction is well-defined by
[[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined]].

inside $B$; it is not the space of all continuous functions on an arbitrary
index set.

Now suppose $W=0$ almost surely and its scale density $g$ is bounded above by $U<\infty$ on $|\sigma-\sigma_0|<\delta$ within $[a,b]$. The support assumption forces $w_0=0$. On $E_R=\{|S_n-n\sigma_0^2|\le R\sqrt n\}$, write $z=(\sigma-\sigma_0)/\sigma_0$. On its full-prior positive-finite set, $(w,x)\mapsto e^{w(x)}/Z_w$ is a jointly measurable density family. The $2r_n$ supremum ball has directional KL at most $2e^{4r_n}r_n^2$ and log-square at most $16r_n^2$ by [F3]. Choose a fixed sufficiently large $k$. Its prior mass is at least $e^{-nr_n^2}$ by [F10], so [F1] at radius $kr_n$ gives a denominator at least $e^{-A nr_n^2}$ for fixed $A=1+2k^2$ except with probability tending to zero.

In binary regression, [F3] places the $2r_n$ prior ball in a directional KL/log-square set of radius $k^2r_n^2$ for a fixed sufficiently large $k$. Its mass is at least $e^{-nr_n^2}$ by [F10], so [F1] gives the same type of denominator bound. For each branch choose $C>1$ larger than its denominator exponent; eventually $e^{-Cnr_n^2}<1/2$. This interval has length at least $1/\sqrt n$ for large $n$, even at an endpoint; [A2] and step 1.2 bound its integral below by $c_R/\sqrt n$ for some $c_R>0$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $\epsilon_n>0$ satisfy $\epsilon_n\to0$ and $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$. For the centered tight Gaussian prior in each branch, let $\mu$ be its law and let $B$ be a separable closed Banach carrier with the norm inherited from that branch's stated function space, as supplied by [[lem-tight-borel-gaussian-law-has-separable-support]]. Write $\mathbb H$ for the covariance RKHS of $\mu$ on $B$, and define
$$\phi_{w_0}(\epsilon)=\inf_{\substack{h\in\mathbb H\\\|h-w_0\|_B<\epsilon}}\left\{\|h\|_{\mathbb H}^2-\log\mu(\epsilon B^\circ)\right\},\qquad \epsilon B^\circ=\{u\in B:\|u\|_B<\epsilon\}.$$

In each branch, parameter-to-data densities are jointly measurable and the posterior $\Pi_n$ is the data-indexed normalization of the prior times the likelihood on fibers with finite positive evidence.

1. **Log-Gaussian density estimation.** On a measurable space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ with sigma-finite measure $\nu$, let $W$ be a tight centered Borel Gaussian random element in $\ell^\infty(\mathsf X)$, and let $w_0$ belong to its support. For IID data $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P_0$, sufficiently large fixed $M$ gives
$$E_0\Pi_n\{w:h(P_w,P_0)>M\epsilon_n\mid X^n\}\longrightarrow0.$$
When $0<\nu(\mathsf X)<\infty$, bounded paths imply the required normalizers are finite and positive.

whose measure property is supplied by

Let $(\mu_k)$ be measures on one measurable space and let $c_k\in[0,+\infty]$. Each scalar multiple $c_k\mu_k$, defined by the zero, finite-positive, and positive-infinity branches of [[def-nonnegative-weighted-sum-of-measures]], is a measure. Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The intervals $I_k$ are disjoint subsets of $[1/2,3/2]$, since $\delta_{k+1}=\delta_k^{k+1}$ and $\delta_{k+1}+\delta_{k+1}^4<\delta_k$. The series $S=\sum_{k\ge k_0}\sqrt{\delta_k}$ is positive and finite, bounded by $\sum_{k\ge k_0}e^{-k/2}$ using $k!\ge k$ and [F3]. Define $$\Pi_\sigma=\tfrac12U_{[1/2,3/2]}+\sum_{k\ge k_0}m_kU_{I_k},\qquad m_k=\frac{\sqrt{\delta_k}}{2S}.$$ By [F2] this is a probability measure with a measurable Lebesgue density bounded below by $1/2$ on the required interval. Its spike densities need not be bounded above near $1$.

The zero Gaussian law is tight and centered, with support $\{0\}$, covariance RKHS $\{0\}$ and $\phi_0(\epsilon)=0$ for every positive $\epsilon$. For all sufficiently large $n$ define $\epsilon_n=\sqrt{\log\log\log n/n}$, choosing arbitrary positive initial terms. Then $\epsilon_n\to0$, $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$ and the concentration condition holds. Put $n_k=\lceil k^4\delta_k^{-2}\rceil$. Since $\log n_k=2k!+O(\log k)$, $\log\log\log n_k=O(\log k)$ and tends to infinity; hence $\epsilon_{n_k}/\delta_k=O(\sqrt{\log k}/k^2)\to0$.

Put $S_n=\sum_iY_i^2$. By [F1] the likelihood ratio relative to true scale $1$ is $$L_n(\sigma)=\exp\{-n\log\sigma+(1-\sigma^{-2})S_n/2\}.$$ On $E_k=\{|S_{n_k}-n_k|\le k\sqrt{n_k}\}$, [F4] gives $P_0(E_k^c)\to0$. Write $q=S_{n_k}/n_k$. Maximizing the log likelihood over all positive $\sigma$ gives its maximum $n_k(q-1-\log q)/2$ at $\sigma^2=q$. Since $|q-1|\le k/\sqrt{n_k}$, Taylor's formula gives $\sup_{\sigma\in[1/2,3/2]}L_{n_k}(\sigma)\le e^{Ck^2}$ for a constant independent of $k$.

Uniformly on $I_k$, $|\sigma-1|\le2\delta_k$. The function $d(\sigma)=-\log\sigma+(1-\sigma^{-2})/2$ satisfies $d(1)=d'(1)=0$ and has bounded second derivative near $1$, while $|1-\sigma^{-2}|\le C|\sigma-1|$. On $E_k$ this gives $$\log L_{n_k}(\sigma)\ge-Cn_k\delta_k^2-Ck\sqrt{n_k}\delta_k\ge-C'k^4.$$ Thus the posterior denominator is at least $m_ke^{-C'k^4}$ on $E_k$.

Fix $M>0$. Since $\epsilon_{n_k}/\delta_k\to0$, the set $J_k=\{|\sigma-1|\le M\epsilon_{n_k}\}$ misses $I_k$ and all earlier spikes for large $k$. Its prior mass is at most $M\epsilon_{n_k}+\sum_{j>k}m_j$. The later sum is $O(\sqrt{\delta_{k+1}})$: successive square-root terms have ratio at most $1/2$ for $k\ge k_0$, so [F3] bounds the tail by twice its first term. Steps 2.1, 3.1 therefore give $$\Pi_\sigma(J_k\mid Y^{n_k})\le e^{Ck^2+C'k^4}\frac{M\epsilon_{n_k}+O(\sqrt{\delta_{k+1}})}{m_k}.$$ Both terms tend to zero: $\epsilon_{n_k}/\sqrt{\delta_k}=O(e^{-k!/2}\sqrt{\log k}/k^2)$ and $\sqrt{\delta_{k+1}/\delta_k}=e^{-kk!/2}$ dominate the polynomial exponent.

On events with probability tending to one, step 4.1 makes posterior mass within $M\epsilon_{n_k}$ tend to zero for every fixed $M$. Thus its expected mass outside that radius tends to one, by boundedness and $P_0(E_k^c)\to0$. The mean function is identically its truth, so this is exactly failure for the combined empirical-mean-plus-scale distance. All original scale-prior and Gaussian concentration assumptions are satisfied, refuting the unrestricted rate claim.
